holidays.name: International Asteroid Day
holidays.description: A global day for looking up, learning about space rocks, and thinking about how humanity could handle a cosmic curveball. Science centers, observatories and space fans mark it with talks, stargazing and livestreams.
holidays.origin: Asteroid Day marks the anniversary of the 1908 Tunguska event, when a space object exploded over Siberia. It was founded in 2015 by astrophysicist Brian May, filmmaker Grig Richters and others. The United Nations later formally recognized it.
holidays.funFact: The Tunguska blast flattened roughly 80 million trees across about 800 square miles, yet no large impact crater was ever found.

holidays.name: Social Media Day
holidays.description: A day to post, comment, reblog and hashtag with abandon, or to try a new platform and meet people you'd never have crossed paths with offline.
holidays.origin: Social Media Day was started by the tech news site Mashable in 2010. It celebrates how online networks have changed the way people communicate, and it has since gone global.
holidays.funFact: The day was created to celebrate online communities at a time when many people still thought of social media as a passing fad.

holidays.name: National Meteor Watch Day
holidays.description: An invitation to grab a blanket, ditch the screens and look up for shooting stars. Dark skies and a little patience are all you need.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance, and its origin is unclear. It falls on the same day as Asteroid Day, which makes for a good night of sky-watching.
holidays.funFact: Most meteors you see are caused by dust grains no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up as they hit the atmosphere at tens of thousands of miles per hour.
